src_lincoln_autobiography_1859.title: Autobiographical Sketch for Jesse W. Fell (1859)
src_lincoln_autobiography_1859.author: Abraham Lincoln
src_lincoln_autobiography_1859.provenance: Library of Congress, Abraham Lincoln Papers, Series 1, December 20, 1859 (public domain).

pages.label: Page 1 — Birth & Virginia Ancestry
pages.text:
Springfield, December 20, 1859.

I was born Feb. 12, 1809, in Hardin County, Kentucky. My parents were both born in Virginia, of undistinguished families—second families, perhaps I should say. My mother, who died in my tenth year, was of a family of the name of Hanks, some of whom now reside in Adams, and others in Macon counties, Illinois.

My paternal grandfather, Abraham Lincoln, emigrated from Rockingham County, Virginia, to Kentucky, about 1781 or 2, where, a year or two later, he was killed by Indians, not in battle, but by stealth, when he was laboring to open a farm in the forest.

pages.label: Page 2 — Indiana Youth & New Salem
pages.text:
My father, at the death of his father, was but six years of age; and he grew up, literally without education. He removed from Kentucky to what is now Spencer County, Indiana, in my eighth year. We reached our new home about the time the State came into the Union.

It was a wild region, with many bears and other wild animals still in the woods. There I grew up. There were some schools, so called; but no qualification was ever required of a teacher, beyond reading, writing, and ciphering to the Rule of Three.

After a flatboat journey to New Orleans, I settled at New Salem on the Sangamon River, where I served as clerk, postmaster, and deputy surveyor.

pages.label: Page 3 — Springfield Law Practice & Family
pages.text:
In 1834 I was elected to the Illinois Legislature, and was re-elected in 1836, 1838, and 1840. During the legislative canvas I studied law from borrowed books.

In the autumn of 1836 I obtained a law license, and on April 15, 1837, removed to Springfield, and commenced the practice, his old friend Stuart taking him into partnership.

On November 4, 1842, I married Mary, daughter of Robert S. Todd, of Lexington, Kentucky. We have had four sons born in Springfield, three of whom are now living.

pages.label: Enumerator Notes — Eighth Street
pages.text:
Archival Comparison (1850 vs. 1860 Federal Schedules):

The August 29, 1850 federal census captures the Eighth Street household six months after the death of second son Edward Baker Lincoln (February 1, 1850) and four months before the birth of William Wallace Lincoln (December 21, 1850).

Mary Ann Todd Lincoln's age is recorded as 28 (she was 31 in August 1850), a typical 19th-century census rounding discrepancy preserved alongside her 1818 Lexington birth record. By July 14, 1860 (M653 Roll 226, p. 113), the family's real estate valuation rose from $3,000 to $5,000 after expanding the residence to two full stories.

src_nara_patent_6469.title: U.S. Patent No. 6,469 — Buoying Vessels Over Shoals (NARA NAID 2524934)
src_nara_patent_6469.author: Abraham Lincoln
src_nara_patent_6469.provenance: National Archives and Records Administration, NAID 2524934, RG 241, Selected Patent Files, May 22, 1849 (public domain).

pages.label: Sheet 1 — Patent Drawing (May 22, 1849)
pages.text:
UNITED STATES PATENT OFFICE.
ABRAHAM LINCOLN, OF SPRINGFIELD, ILLINOIS.
MANNER OF BUOYING VESSELS.
Specification of Letters Patent No. 6,469, dated May 22, 1849.

To all whom it may concern:
Be it known that I, ABRAHAM LINCOLN, of Springfield, in the county of Sangamon, in the State of Illinois, have invented a new and improved manner of combining adjustable buoyant air chambers with a steam boat or other vessel for the purpose of enabling their draught of water to be readily lessened to enable them to pass over bars, or through shallow water, without discharging their cargoes.

pages.label: Sheet 2 — Signed Petition (NARA Scan)
pages.text:
To the Commissioner of Patents:

The petition of Abraham Lincoln, of Springfield in the County of Sangamon & State of Illinois, respectfully represents:
That your petitioner has invented a new and improved manner of combining adjustable buoyant air chambers with steam boats or other vessels, which he verily believes has not been known or used prior to the invention thereof by your petitioner.

Signed: Abraham Lincoln, March 10, 1849.
National Archives Identifier (NAID): 2524934, Record Group 241.

src_lincoln_scripps_1860.title: Campaign Autobiography for John Locke Scripps (June 1860)
src_lincoln_scripps_1860.author: Abraham Lincoln
src_lincoln_scripps_1860.provenance: Library of Congress, Abraham Lincoln Papers, Series 1, June 1860 (public domain).

pages.label: Page 1 — Berks County, Pennsylvania & Virginia Roots
pages.text:
Abraham Lincoln was born Feb. 12, 1809, then in Hardin, now in the more recently formed county of Larue, Kentucky.

His father, Thomas, & grandfather, Abraham, were born in Rockingham county Virginia, whither their ancestors had come from Berks county Pennsylvania. His lineage has been traced no farther back than this.

The family were originally quakers, though in later times they have fallen away from the peculiar habits of that people. (Note: Later parish and probate research proved the earlier four generations back to Hingham, Massachusetts and Hingham, Norfolk, England in 1622.)

pages.label: Page 2 — The 1830 Illinois Migration & Black Hawk War
pages.text:
March 1st. 1830—Abraham having just completed his 21st. year, his father and family, with the families of the two daughters and sons-in-law, of his step-mother, left the old homestead in Indiana, and came to Illinois.

Their mode of conveyance was waggons drawn by ox-teams, and Abraham drove one of the teams. They reached the county of Macon, and stopped there some time within the same month of March.

In the spring of 1832 the Black-Hawk war broke out; and Abraham joined a volunteer company, and to his own surprize, was elected captain of it.

src_nara_emancipation_1863.title: Emancipation Proclamation (NARA NAID 299998)
src_nara_emancipation_1863.author: President Abraham Lincoln
src_nara_emancipation_1863.provenance: National Archives and Records Administration, NAID 299998, RG 11, Presidential Proclamations, January 1, 1863 (public domain).

pages.label: Page 1 — Manuscript Proclamation (NARA Scan)
pages.text:
By the President of the United States of America:
A Proclamation.

Whereas, on the twenty-second day of September, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and sixty-two, a proclamation was issued by the President of the United States...

I do order and declare that all persons held as slaves within said designated States, and parts of States, are, and henceforward shall be free; and that the Executive government of the United States, including the military and naval authorities thereof, will recognize and maintain the freedom of said persons.

Done at the City of Washington, this first day of January, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and sixty three.
By the President: ABRAHAM LINCOLN.
